cards.body: Most personal software is someone else's app: its screens, its data model, its server. If you want a grocery list that knows your recipes, a log of your car's maintenance, and your photo feed in one place, you either accept several apps that don't talk to each other or you write and ship your own app, for every platform, and keep it updated.
cards.heading: The problem

cards.body:
Split an app into three parts and give each one a single owner:

- **What the screens look like and what data they show** lives on a server you own, the **pod**, as data: JSON trees called **layouts**.
- **Drawing** happens on your devices, in one native renderer that knows how to draw any layout but nothing about any particular app.
- **Building** is done by your **agent**: Claude connects to the pod and writes layouts and data definitions for you, checked by the pod on every write.

So changing your grocery screen means the agent writes a new layout to the pod, and every device shows it a moment later. No app store, no build, no release.
cards.heading: The answer

cards.body:
```
 your agent (Claude)
        │ MCP
        ▼
 pod (your server) ◀──▶ the web,
        │               Pixelfed, …
        │ layouts + data,
        │ live events
        ▼
 engine + renderer on each device
 (desktop, Android, web, simulator)
```
cards.heading: In one picture

cards.body: Each user has their own pod: one SQLite database with their data, their layouts and their sign-ins to other services. Tokens for those services are sealed at rest and never reach a device. A pod can be exported whole, and a collection's data can be exported row by row.
cards.heading: Your data stays yours

cards.body: Screens are drawn natively by a Rust renderer (GPU or CPU), not in a web view. Everything a device has loaded is cached, so the app opens and scrolls with no network. A tap changes the screen at once and is queued to be sent when the network returns.
cards.heading: Native and offline first

cards.body: The core of the system is generic: it handles layouts, entities and actions in general, never a particular app. A new screen or a new data source is server code and layout files, so it reaches users without a client release. Only new **vocabulary** (a new kind of node the renderer must learn to draw) needs a new client build.
cards.heading: Most changes ship from the server alone

cards.body: A new pod is a blank home screen. Your agent adds only what you ask for, through the pod's MCP server. The pod validates every write, keeps every version so any change can be undone, and draws previews so the agent can look at what it made.
cards.heading: Your agent builds, only what you ask

cards.body: A phone that hasn't updated must still draw something sensible. Every piece of vocabulary is a named **feature**; a client says which features it can draw, and the pod serves it the newest version of each layout that uses only those.
cards.heading: Old clients keep working

cards.body: The pod reaches other hosts only through a client that refuses private network addresses. Text that other people wrote (web pages, shared layouts, tool output) is marked as data, never instructions, before an agent sees it. Anything shared with another person is reviewed first.
cards.heading: Safe by default

cards.body: There is no app store and no "installing an app". A pod has **layouts**, starting with `home`, which the clients open first; home embeds or opens every other layout. Built-in screens (Pixelfed, Events, Settings, the inbox) are **core layouts** the server ships, which your layouts reference or copy (decisions `layouts-not-apps`, `blueprints-and-home`).
cards.heading: No apps, only layouts

cards.body: A layout says what to draw and what each tap sends, nothing more. It binds fields of entities (`$item.title`), shows or hides things on simple conditions, and attaches **intents** ("change this field and send it to this endpoint"). Anything that needs real logic lives in a source on the pod, in Rust.
cards.heading: No logic in layouts

cards.body: The renderer is Rust from layout to pixels. The web client is the same renderer compiled to WebAssembly and drawn into a canvas; it is not HTML.
cards.heading: No web view

cards.body:
```
 agent (Claude)    websites, Pixelfed,
      │ MCP        models, runners
      ▼                  ▲
┌─ server ───────────────┼───────┐
│ host: pods, tokens, scheduler  │
│ ┌─ pod ──────────────────────┐ │
│ │ the construct · sessions · │ │
│ │ notifications              │ │
│ │ sources: collections,      │ │
│ │ pixelfed, events, agents,  │ │
│ │ taste, shell, monitor,     │ │
│ │ dates                      │ │
│ │ jacks: model, web,         │ │
│ │ web_search, mcp, accounts  │ │
│ └────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────▲─────────────────┬───────┘
       │ HTTP: construct,│ SSE:
       │ objects, data,  │ construct,
       │ actions         ▼ data, …
┌─ each device ──────────────────┐
│ engine: cache, outbox,         │
│ sign-in, event stream          │
├────────────────────────────────┤
│ renderer: layout → pixels      │
├────────────────────────────────┤
│ desktop · Android · web ·      │
│ simulator · previews           │
└────────────────────────────────┘
```
cards.heading: The whole system

cards.body:
| Piece | Crates | Its job |
|---|---|---|
| **Host** | `pod-host`, `server` | One server process holding many pods: which token opens which pod, temporary pods, waking pods that have work due, what pods share |
| **Pod** | `pod-core` | One user's server: their layouts, data, sessions, sign-ins and notifications, and the HTTP and MCP endpoints |
| **Sources** | `source-*` | Everything specific to one kind of data: Collections, Pixelfed, Events, Agents, … The pod knows them only through one trait, `Source` |
| **Jacks and modules** | `pod_core::jacks`, `web-extract`, `agent` | The abilities a pod is plugged into (a model, the web, search, accounts), and the two modules every web request and model call go through |
| **The construct** | `construct-elements`, `protocol` | The pod's layouts and components as content-addressed elements, and the vocabulary they are written in |
| **Engine** | `client-core` | The device's brain: a local cache, an outbox of changes, sign-in, and the live event stream |
| **Renderer and clients** | `construct-render`, `construct-web`, `construct-sim` | Draws any layout; the desktop, Android and web apps, the headless simulator and the pod's previews are all this one renderer |
| **Agent** | (outside) | Claude, connected to the pod's MCP server, builds layouts and collections |
cards.heading: The pieces in one line each

cards.body:
1. **The device opens a pod.** The user typed a pod code once; the engine traded it for a pod session (`POST /v1/pods/open`) and keeps that session in the platform's secure store.
2. **It asks for the root.** `GET /v1/construct` answers the hash of `home` as this device can draw it, given the features it sent in `X-Construct-Features`.
3. **It fetches what it lacks.** `POST /v1/objects {have, want}` answers the elements (layouts, components) home reaches that the device doesn't already hold. Elements are immutable and named by hash, so anything already cached is never fetched again.
4. **It loads the data.** `GET /v1/construct/data/<element>` answers a **data bundle**: the entities the layout binds, keyed by URI, and the queries (ordered lists of URIs) its lists draw. The pod asks each source for its feeds.
5. **It draws.** The renderer lays the layout out, binds each `$item.field` to the cached entities, and paints.
6. **It stays live.** `GET /v1/construct/events` stays open: a `construct` event when any layout changes, a `data` event when data changes, a `notification` event when something arrives.
cards.heading: Step by step

cards.body: The renderer knew layouts and entities, never "Pixelfed". The engine knew URLs, hashes and JSON, never what a post is. The pod knew which source fills each feed; only the source knew how to talk to the outside service.
cards.heading: What each piece knew

cards.body:
1. **The tap.** The layout's heart button carries an intent:
   ```json
   {"intent": "action.mutation.optimistic", "entity_uri": "$item.uri", "field": "is_liked",
    "value_expr": "!entity.is_liked", "endpoint": "/v1/pixelfed/posts/like", "payload": {"id": "$item.id"}}
   ```
   The renderer binds `$item` and hands the intent to the engine.
2. **Optimistic change.** The engine flips `is_liked` in its cache and writes the request to its **outbox** in the same database transaction. The screen redraws: the heart is red before any network call.
3. **Sending.** A background worker sends outbox rows oldest first. A 2xx removes the row; a 4xx removes it and rolls the change back; a 5xx, a timeout or no network keeps it and retries with backoff. A row the pod has kept answering with an error for 10 minutes is given up (rolled back like a 4xx) so the rows behind it are sent, and the device says which (decision `failing-saves-give-up`).
4. **The pod.** The route `/v1/pixelfed/posts/like` belongs to the Pixelfed source, which the pod mounted. The source calls Pixelfed's API with the token it keeps sealed in the pod.
5. **Back to every device.** The source tells the pod its data changed; the pod sends a `data` event to every open stream, and other devices reload just that data.
cards.heading: Step by step

cards.body:
| Seam | Between | What crosses it |
|---|---|---|
| **The `Source` trait** (`pod_core::Source`) | pod ↔ each source | A manifest of feeds, data paths and actions; feed data; routes; tables; notifications; jacks; core layouts and components |
| **The construct API** (HTTP) | engine ↔ pod | `GET /v1/construct` (the root), `POST /v1/objects` (elements by hash), `GET /v1/construct/data/<el>` (a data bundle), source routes for actions |
| **The event stream** (SSE) | pod → engine | `construct`, `data`, `notification` and `notifications_read` events |
| **Features** (`X-Construct-Features`) | engine → pod | The vocabulary a device can draw, so the pod serves layouts it can draw |
| **The layout vocabulary** (`protocol`) | pod, engine, renderer | Node types (`core://Text`, `core://List`, …), intents (`action.*`), bindings, device data |
| **MCP** (`POST /v1/mcp`) | agent ↔ pod | Tools to read sources, write layouts and collections, preview, share |
| **`Loader` and `Platform`** (`construct-render`) | renderer ↔ its host | How the renderer gets layouts and data, and what it asks of the operating system |
| **Jacks** (`pod_core::jacks`) | features ↔ abilities | Whether the pod may use a model, the web, search or an account, and their settings |
cards.heading: The interfaces

cards.body: Each seam is a promise that lets one side change without the other. A source can change everything about how it talks to Pixelfed without touching the pod. The pod can change how it stores layouts without touching the engine, as long as the construct API holds. A renderer can learn new tricks without the pod knowing, as long as it says so in its features.
cards.heading: Why narrow seams

cards.body: The engine, the renderer and `pod-core` handle layouts, entities and intents in general (decisions D34, D35, D40). Everything specific to Pixelfed is in `crates/source-pixelfed`, and so on; a test (`the_core_names_no_source`) fails if the core names a source. That is what lets product changes ship without client releases.
cards.heading: The core knows no source

cards.body: The vocabulary has two layers (decision `plumbing-and-porcelain`). **Plumbing** is what the renderer draws: nodes, intents and device data, each a named feature, and adding to it needs a client build. **Porcelain** is **components**: pieces of layout defined as data in terms of plumbing, expanded before drawing, so adding or changing one needs no client build.
cards.heading: Plumbing and porcelain

cards.body: Core layouts and server components are append-only numbered files (`NNNN.json`): a deployed file is never edited, and the server refuses to start if one changed. The pod keeps every version of every layout behind its name. Database schemas change only by migrations that work on existing pods. Decisions are recorded, never rewritten.
cards.heading: History is kept, not rewritten

cards.body:
Each pod is `pods/<id>/server.db`:

- **The construct**: every layout and component element, and the names that point at them with their history.
- **Sessions**: the pod sessions of devices and of the web client, and MCP credentials for agents.
- **Sign-ins**: tokens for upstream services (a Pixelfed account, an agent runner), sealed with the server's key.
- **Source data**: each source's own tables (`<source>_*`): a collection's rows, Pixelfed's cursors, the Agents mirror.
- **Notifications** and the devices registered for push.
- **Jacks**: which abilities are plugged in, with sealed settings.
cards.heading: What a pod holds

cards.body:
- **To devices**: the construct API and event stream, the data bundles, the sources' action routes, uploads, notifications.
- **To the agent**: the MCP server at `/v1/mcp`.
- **To nobody else**: a caller without a pod token sees only an "Open your pod" screen.
cards.heading: What a pod serves

cards.body:
The host's own database lists the pods and what crosses between them:

- `pods`: each pod's id, name, kind (`admin` or `temporary`), expiry, and `next_wake_at`.
- `credentials`: the SHA-256 of each pod token (`cpod_…`), MCP credential and web session. Tokens themselves are never stored.
- The **shelf**: handles, publications and their objects (what pods share with each other).
- `public_copies` and `calendar_feeds`: public web links and `.ics` feeds.
- OAuth clients and codes, for agents that connect with OAuth.
cards.heading: host.db

cards.body:
- **Routing**: a request's bearer token names its pod; the host opens that pod lazily on its first request.
- **Temporary pods**: `POST /v1/pods/temporary` makes a 24-hour pod for trying a server, deleted afterwards, with risky jacks locked off.
- **The scheduler**: every 30 seconds it opens pods whose `next_wake_at` is due (notification polls, collection fillers, reminders). A pod polls upstreams only while it has a device seen in the last 30 days, so idle pods cost nothing.
- **OAuth for agents**, connected apps, public media under `/v1/p/<pod>/…`, the web client at `/web` (also loaded by the owner's own sites, decision `site-origins`), and public links at `/s/…` and `/<handle>/<slug>`.
cards.heading: What the host does

cards.body: `crates/server` compiles in the sources (`server::adapters()`: Pixelfed, Events, the shell layouts, Collections, Monitor, Agents, Dates) and runs `server serve`. Its other subcommands manage pods: `server pods create`, `rotate`, `delete`, `mcp` (an MCP credential), `monitoring on`, `gaps`, and `server backup <dir>`. Configuration is `CONSTRUCT_*` environment variables ([server.md](https://github.com/aidanwolter3/the-construct/blob/main/docs/server.md)).
cards.heading: The server binary

cards.body:
| Job | Modules |
|---|---|
| Sources | `adapter` (the `Source` trait), `source` (manifests, matching paths and query keys), `static_app` (a source that is only layouts) |
| The construct | `construct` and `construct_*` (store, write, seal, events, HTTP, share, adopted, trace), `components`, `porcelain`, `layouts`, `validate`, `hints` |
| Devices | `session` (pod sessions, sign-ins), `notify`, `notify_store`, `push` (Web Push), `devices`, `uploads`, `image_proxy` |
| Agents | `mcp` (the pod's MCP server), `preview` (drawing layouts for the agent), `mcp_servers` (the pod as an MCP client) |
| Abilities | `jacks`, `net` (the outbound HTTP client), `secrets` (sealing) |
| Sharing outward | `public_copy` (public links), `ical` (calendar feeds) |
| Plumbing | `store` and `migrations` (SQLite and named migration steps), `tz`, `metrics`, `disk` |
cards.heading: The modules by job

cards.body: `pod_core::app` builds one axum router: the core routes (`/v1/construct…`, `/v1/objects`, `/v1/notifications…`, `/v1/devices…`, `/v1/uploads`, `/v1/jacks…`, `/v1/mcp`, `/v1/auth…`) plus each source's own router under `/v1/<source>/…`. Every handler gets the same state, `Pod` (an `Arc<AppState>`), which also gives a source its store, its catalog of sources, per-pod values, and `publish_data` to say its data changed.
cards.heading: The router

cards.body: A source that pulls from an upstream implements `Source::poll_interval` and `poll_notifications`. Pixelfed polls its notifications every two minutes; Collections uses the same poll to run scheduled fills and send due reminders; Monitor checks its health every five. After a poll the pod records when it next needs waking in `host.db` (`next_wake_at`). Failed polls back off from a minute to an hour.
cards.heading: Polls

cards.body: `Source::resume` restarts background jobs when a pod opens (an upload that was still posting). `Source::keeps_open` asks the host to keep the pod open from server start: the Agents source does, to follow its runner's event stream without waiting for a request.
cards.heading: Resuming and staying open

cards.body: Pod tokens are stored as hashes. Upstream tokens and jack secrets are sealed at rest with the server's key (`CONSTRUCT_SECRETS_KEY`) and never sent to a device. A credential issued to an agent reaches only `/v1/mcp`, and only at the access its owner gave it: read, edit, or outward (sharing publicly, starting agent runs, reaching new hosts, deleting). Every tool is checked against it before it runs, and rows the agent writes below outward count as the agent's, not the owner's (decision `mcp-access-levels`). A credential for an unattended job can carry a **grant** as well: its exact tools, the collections whose rows it may write, where it may delete, screens it may never change, the collections it may read, and whether its answers withhold what others wrote. The pod enforces it inside every write transaction and on every read tool, and adds what no grant may reach: screens the pod shares, rows a calendar feed reads, any web host the pod's screens don't already use, and a card address that isn't one of the pod's own screens (decision `mcp-grants`). The pod logs every call a credential makes, refusals included, where the job can't write; three refusals in an hour raise a warning, and the owner can undo a morning's background work in one step (decision `mcp-call-log`).
cards.heading: Secrets

cards.body: Every request a pod makes to a host a user chose goes through `pod_core::net`'s outbound client, which resolves names itself and refuses private and internal addresses; a lint (`clippy.toml`) forbids building another HTTP client. Web pages are fetched through the web module, which adds per-host spacing, daily caps and backoff (Part 6).
cards.heading: Outbound requests

cards.body: Text other people wrote (a web page, a shared layout, an MCP server's tool description) reaches the agent wrapped as `{"untrusted": {"from", "content"}}`, and the pod's instructions say it is data, never instructions (decision `untrusted-tool-content`). Sharing anything outward (a publication, a public link, a calendar feed) answers a review of exactly what would go out, and nothing goes until it is confirmed.
cards.heading: Outside text is data

cards.body:
```json
{"type": "core://Page", "id": "c-groceries1", "title": "Groceries",
 "root": {"type": "core://Column", "padding_h_dp": 20, "children": [
   {"type": "core://Text", "style": "Title", "value_expr": "Groceries"},
   {"type": "core://List", "query_key": "collection:groceries",
    "where": {"field": "deleted", "equals": "false"},
    "item_template": {"type": "core://Row", "children": [
      {"type": "core://Switch", "checked": "$item.done",
       "on_click": {"intent": "action.mutation.optimistic", "entity_uri": "$item.uri",
                    "field": "done", "value_expr": "!entity.done",
                    "endpoint": "/v1/collections/groceries/update",
                    "payload": {"id": "$item.id", "done": "$value"}}},
      {"type": "core://Text", "value_expr": "$item.name"}]}}]}}
```

The list draws every entity of the query `collection:groceries`; each row binds `$item` to one entity; the switch's intent flips `done` at once and sends the change.
cards.heading: A small layout

cards.body: A layout's root is a `core://Page`: any node, with nothing drawn around it by the app, so the layout draws its own header and Back. A page can declare **screens**, opened by route: a tap with `target_uri: "collections://groceries/r1"` opens the screen whose `route` is `collections://groceries/{id}`, and `$route.id` is `r1` inside it. Older layouts may be a `core://Workspace`, which is porcelain the pod expands into a page.
cards.heading: Pages and screens

cards.body:
| Family | Nodes |
|---|---|
| Structure | `Page`, `Layout` (another layout, embedded or as a sheet or panel), `Scroll`, `Sticky`, `Dock`, `Drawer`, `AppFrame` |
| Arrangement | `Column`, `Row`, `Box` (a surface with padding, colour, border, corners), `Container`, `Spacer`, `Divider` |
| Content | `Text` (with styles, dates, counts and Markdown), `Image`, `Badge`, `Chip`, `Progress`, `Bars` (a chart) |
| Data | `List` (a query's entities through a template, filtered, grouped, in columns or a stack), `Carousel`, `Conditional` |
| Controls | `Button`, `IconButton`, `Tappable`, `Gesture`, `SwipeCard`, `Switch`, `TextField`, `ChoiceChips`, `MediaPicker` |

All are `core://<Name>`. A node type a client doesn't know is skipped and kept, so old versions still parse.
cards.heading: Nodes

cards.body: `action.navigation.open` (a screen, or another layout pushed, as a sheet, panel or overlay), `.back`, `.pop_to`, `.pop_to_root`; `action.mutation.optimistic` and `action.mutation.create` (change or add data at once, sent through the outbox); `action.local.set` (view state on this device only); `action.form.clear` (empty form boxes after an Add, typing going on); `action.sequence`, `action.confirm`, `action.link.open`, `action.data.load`; `action.device` (something only the device does: sign in, sign out, mark notifications read, leave the pod).
cards.heading: Intents

cards.body: `$item.<field>` reads the current row, `${<uri>#<field>}` any entity, `$route.<name>` a screen's route, `$form.<field>` a text field's value, `$nonce` a fresh id per tap. Mutations compute the new value with a tiny expression language (`!entity.done`, `entity.count + 1`, `a ? b : c`). **Device data** is what the device knows itself, with no pod request: `local://connection` (online, pending changes), `local://inbox`, `local://theme` (the pod's colours), `local://device` (window size), `local://nav` (where the layout is drawn).
cards.heading: Bindings and device data

cards.body:
```json
{"type": "core://Use", "ref": "@core/card", "args": {"spacing": 6}, "children": [
  {"type": "core://Text", "style": "Label", "value_expr": "$item.title"}]}
```

Names say where a component comes from:

- `@core/<name>`: shipped with the server, in `crates/pod-core/components/<name>/NNNN.json` or a source's own `components/` folder. Every core layout is one too (`@core/events`), and so is each of its parts (`@core/pixelfed/screen:post`).
- `@me/<name>`: the pod's own, defined by the agent (`define_component`) or copied from a core one (`copy_component`).

Older layouts spell these `core:<name>` and `pod:<name>`; a write still accepts them.
cards.heading: Using one

cards.body: A definition is `{doc, params, children?, template, examples}`. In the template, `$arg.<name>` is an argument, `core://Children` is where the caller's children go (or a named slot), `core://IfArg` and `core://Match` choose a branch, and `core://Each` repeats a piece per entry of a list argument. Every example must expand to valid plumbing, or the write is refused. `crates/construct-elements` does the expanding, for the pod and the engine alike.
cards.heading: Defining one

cards.body:
- An **element** is `e1-` and the base32 SHA-256 of its canonical JSON (keys sorted, no whitespace). It never changes.
- A **name** (`home`, `c-…` for the pod's layouts, `@me/…`, `@core/…`) points at an element and keeps every element it pointed at before: that is the undo history (`restore_version`).
- A **reference** sits at one of three sites: a `core://Use` (a component, expanded in place), a `core://Layout` (an embed) and an `action.navigation.open` (a link). Written as a name, it is **sealed** to `{el, name, pin}`. An unpinned reference follows its name: when the name moves, the pod seals every element that follows it again, up to home.
cards.heading: Elements, names and references

cards.body: Embeds and links are **edges**, keyed by their `as` or their name. From home, the edges say which layouts a user can reach and how (MCP `list_layouts` answers each layout's `reached` path). Writes that would make a layout reach itself are refused, so the graph only goes forward; Back and `pop_to` go the other way.
cards.heading: Edges and reach

cards.body: The engine asks for the root as a **manifest** of names and hashes, fetches the objects it lacks with `POST /v1/objects`, keeps them in its store (a restart with the same root fetches nothing), and expands components itself with `construct-elements`. A layout home doesn't reach (one a notification opens) is fetched by name with `GET /v1/construct/names/<name>`.
cards.heading: How a device syncs

cards.body:
- Each feature is a file, `crates/protocol/features/<name>.md` (about a hundred), and `protocol::required_features` works out which features a node tree uses.
- A client sends every feature it draws in `X-Construct-Features`.
- When the pod **seals** a root for that client, it picks, for every name, the newest entry of its history that uses nothing the client lacks and nothing removed.
cards.heading: How it works

cards.body: Adding a node type or field needs a client build: the type in `protocol`, a feature file, an arm in `required_features`, drawing it in `construct-render`, and tests (`crates/protocol/features/README.md`). Removing one never edits layouts: its file moves to `features/removed/`, and only elements that use it are retired.
cards.heading: Adding and removing vocabulary

cards.body: Core layouts are the screens the server ships: `pixelfed`, `events`, `agents`, `taste` (with `taste_item`, a piece as a sheet), `server_health`, `shell` (the blank home), `settings`, `inbox`, and the `checklist` kit. Each is a folder of append-only files in its source's crate, `crates/source-*/layouts/<id>/NNNN.json`; when a pod opens, each `@core/<id>` name moves to this build's newest file. The server builds those files into elements once, for the first pod it opens, and every later pod moves to the same ones. A pod's layout can use a core layout whole by reference (`{"type": "core://Use", "ref": "@core/events"}`), which then follows every deploy, or copy it, which doesn't.
cards.heading: Core layouts

cards.body: The agent's layouts are names `c-` plus ten characters, each with a title, an icon and a root node (at most 50 layouts, 256 KiB each). Home embeds a layout in place (`core://Layout` `Inline`), in a card, or as a sheet or panel while a condition holds, and opens others (`action.navigation.open` with a layout: pushed, a sheet, a panel, an overlay from any edge). **Home owns the feeds**: it lists the data feeds the pod's layouts may bind, and every write is validated against what those feeds' sources declare.
cards.heading: The pod's layouts

cards.body: Because a copy doesn't follow its core layout, fixing a core layout may not reach a user who copied it. MCP `list_layouts` marks each layout's `copy_of` and `reached` (decision `trace-from-home`), so a change goes to the element home actually reaches.
cards.heading: Change what the user sees

cards.body: `publish` copies a name's closure (everything it embeds, links and uses) to the host's **shelf**, turning each collection it reads into an **input** with the fields it needs. Another pod `adopt`s the share link, binding each input to one of its own collections. An adopted element reaches only the data it is bound to, and anything risky it would do (start agent runs, plug jacks, delete, sign out) waits for the user's yes (decisions `sharing`, `adoption-capabilities`).
cards.heading: Publications and adoption

cards.body: `share_publicly` makes a read-only copy of a layout, the layouts it opens, and only the Collections rows they show, served as a web page at `/s/pub-…` or `/<handle>/<slug>` and drawn by the web client, also on the owner's own site (decision `site-origins`). Buttons that write are taken out. The copy is refreshed when its rows change; new rows wait for a new review unless the link says to publish them (decisions `public-web-links`, `public-links-share-the-closure`).
cards.heading: Public links
The manifest

cards.body:
| Group | Methods |
|---|---|
| Identity and data | `name` (also its table and route prefix), `manifest`, `feed` (answers a feed's data), `has_feed` |
| Routes and storage | `router`, `public_paths`, `migrations` (its `<name>_*` tables), `on_open` |
| Shipping layouts | `core_layouts`, `layout_files`, `component_files`, `element_catalog` |
| Sign-in | `sign_ins`, `sign_in_start`, `sign_in_account`, `share_sign_in` |
| Notifications | `notification_channels`, `poll_interval`, `poll_notifications`, `notification_store` |
| Background | `resume`, `keeps_open` |
| Jacks | `jacks`, `jack_status`, `unplug_jack` |
| The agent | `mcp_tools`, `mcp_call`, `mcp_instructions`, `check_custom_layout` |
| Sharing | `public_data`, `calendar_events`, `share_inputs`, `adopted_scope`, `data_sets` |

Almost every method has a default, so a small source implements only `name`, `manifest`, `feed`, `core_layouts` and `layout_files`.
cards.heading: The rest of the trait

cards.body:
```json
{"entities": {"collections://groceries/r1": {"id": "r1", "name": "Milk", "done": false}},
 "queries":  {"collection:groceries": ["collections://groceries/r1"]}}
```

Entities are shared across screens: two lists showing the same post show the same cached entity, so a like on one shows on both. A feed's data, a screen's data path and a create's answer all have this shape (`protocol::DataBundle`).
cards.heading: The bundle

cards.body: When a source's data changes it calls `publish_data` on the pod, which sends a `data` event on every open stream, usually naming what changed (a collection's rows, URI prefixes, query keys). The engine reloads only cached data that matches, what's on screen first (decision `scoped-data-events`).
cards.heading: Data events

cards.body: A collection has typed fields: `text`, `number`, `bool`, `date`, `datetime`, `choice`, `ref` (a row of another collection), `quantity` ("1 1/2 cups"). Rows are `collections://<c>/<id>` in the query `collection:<c>`, with routes to create, update, delete and export them. Fields have permanent ids, so renames keep an alias, removals are restorable for 30 days, and a write from an offline device made under an older definition still lands.
cards.heading: Fields and rows

cards.body:
- **Computed fields**: `expr` (a small expression), `lookup` (a value from another collection, kept as editable rules), `count` and `rollup` (over rows that point here), `model` (a model's answer, in the background). Lookups and counts are live: a change to the rows they read recomputes what it affects.
- **Views**: small derived lists (`collection:<c>:view:<v>`), filtered, dated ("upcoming") and limited.
- **Actions**: insert-from-query, update-all and delete-all actions a button can run (add a recipe to the grocery list).
- **Fillers**: keep rows current from the web: `fetch` (a URL, an extractor, a field map: no model per fill), `agent` (a model with search researches the rows), `range` (one row per day of a moving window), `mcp` (a remote MCP server's tool).
- **Alerts and reminders**: notify once when a row matches, or when a date field is reached.
cards.heading: What else a collection can do

cards.body: Every pod's notifications are rows of its `notifications` collection (decision `notifications-in-a-collection`), so a layout lists them like any data and the agent can edit them. Collections provides the pod's notification store.
cards.heading: Notifications live here

cards.body:
- Entities `pixelfed://posts/…`, `users/…`, `media/…`; feed `home` (query `timeline:home`).
- Screen data: a post, its comments. Actions: like, bookmark, comment, create a post, retry or discard one.
- An OAuth sign-in to any instance (`/v1/auth/pixelfed/…`), and the `pixelfed` account jack.
- Notification channels (likes, comments, mentions, follows), polled every two minutes.
- The `pixelfed` core layout and its components; a sample layout that needs no sign-in for the simulator.
cards.heading: What it declares

cards.body: Posting photos crosses every piece: the device stages photos, the engine uploads them (`POST /v1/uploads`) and queues the create, the pod claims the uploads, and the source posts them to Pixelfed, resuming after a restart ([posting.md](https://github.com/aidanwolter3/the-construct/blob/main/docs/posting.md)).
cards.heading: Posting

cards.body: Events (`crates/source-events`) has no data of its own: it is the system collection `events`, each website the user watches is a fetch filler, and each rule an alert. It ships the `events` core layout and the `matches` notification channel.
cards.heading: Events

cards.body:
Agents (`crates/source-agents`) mirrors an external **agent runner** that runs Claude Code on cloud sandboxes, over the runner's protocol (CAP v3: a snapshot, a resumable event stream, actions). The pod owns the work (Tasks rows, schedules) and notifications; the runner owns the runs and their outcomes. It keeps its pod open to follow the stream ([agents.md](https://github.com/aidanwolter3/the-construct/blob/main/docs/agents.md)).

Two of the pod's schedules are **Anticipate**: every morning one reads the day ahead and one walks the owner's journeys through their real screens. Writes in those walks are dry runs. A fix is staged as an edit group, walked staged, and applied only when the server finds it safe (nothing lost, nothing new done) and unprotected; the owner undoes or redoes it in one tap, and the device swaps the screen at once from both versions the manifest lists. When the day calls for it, it also reshapes the owner's Today for the day and the week, as a one-day trial they can keep ([anticipate.md](https://github.com/aidanwolter3/the-construct/blob/main/docs/anticipate.md)).
cards.heading: Agents

cards.body: Taste (`crates/source-taste`) shows the feed of the owner's own **taste service**, which ranks clothes from real stores to find the edges of what they like. The pod signs in to it with a URL and token like the agents runner, keeps the feed it was served (the service answers a new page every time it is asked, and a layout's feed is fetched again after every data event) and deals it as a deck of swipe cards, passing likes and skips on and fetching the next page itself when few are left; the item, search, taste and map screens are read from the service when they are shown. The owner's likes and dislikes are the pod's: every request names the pod's history, the service keeps a copy of it, and a service that lacks the version named is sent it whole (decision `taste-history-in-the-pod`). The map is a scatter of the whole catalog (`core://Scatter`, decision `scatter-and-tap-paging`): tap a dot to open its piece, drag a box to list the pieces in it; a tile grid stays for clients without it ([taste.md](https://github.com/aidanwolter3/the-construct/blob/main/docs/taste.md)).
cards.heading: Taste

cards.body:
- **Shell** (`crates/source-shell`): layouts only. `shell`, the blank home; `settings`; and `inbox`.
- **Monitor** (`crates/source-monitor`): the server's health counters and checks (feed `overview`, for pods the operator turned it on for), the user's devices with their builds (feed `devices`) and the pod's own recent failed requests (feed `errors`: route pattern, status, error code, device; kept in memory per pod by `pod_core::recent_errors`, decision `recent-server-errors`) and this month's paid use, the pod's and the server's (feed `paid_use`, kept by `pod_core::paid_use`, decision `monthly-paid-use`), with the `server_health` core layout.
- **Dates** (`crates/source-dates`): the days around today in the pod's time zone (`dates:today`, `dates:this_week`, `dates:next_7`, …), so a layout that lists days needs no collection of dates. It tells devices to reload at the pod's midnight.
cards.heading: Shell, Monitor and Dates

cards.body:
```
upstream
   │ poll
   ▼
source ── a notification:
   │      channel, title,
   │      body, target_uri
   ▼
pod: stored once, in the
notifications collection
   ├─▶ `notification` event
   │   on open streams
   └─▶ Web Push to devices
          │
          ▼
device: inbox, badge, OS
notification ─ tap ─▶ its
layout, then its screen
```
cards.heading: The path

cards.body: Only the source knows where a notification came from. The pod, the engine and the clients see a channel ("Likes"), title and body text, a `target_uri`, and the layout to present it in, which the pod picks: the first of the pod's layouts with a screen whose route matches the target ([notifications.md](https://github.com/aidanwolter3/the-construct/blob/main/docs/notifications.md)).
cards.heading: Who knows what

cards.body: `pod_core::jacks` defines `JackSpec {id, title, summary, kind}`, with `JackKind::Switch {default_on}`, `Config {fields}` and `Account {how}`. State is a row of the pod's `jacks` table; a host locks one with `jack.<id> = locked` in the pod's settings. Code asks `is_plugged(pod, id)` (or `config(store, id)` for a config jack's values, secrets opened). Claude plugs jacks with MCP (`list_jacks`, `plug_jack`, `unplug_jack`); people do in Settings → Jacks.
cards.heading: The interface

cards.body:
| Jack | Kind | Enables |
|---|---|---|
| `model` | switch, on | Computed fields that ask a model, fillers that read pages or research, picks from search results |
| `web` | switch, on | Fetching websites: fillers, Events' sites, previews |
| `web_search` | config: `brave` + key, `searxng` + URL, or `duckduckgo` | `query_field` fillers and the search tool of agent fills |
| `mcp` | switch, on | Calling tools of the remote MCP servers the pod is connected to |
| `pixelfed` | account | The Pixelfed source |
| `agent_runner` | account | The Agents source |
| `taste` | account | The Taste source |
cards.heading: The jacks today

cards.body:
- `fetch`: a capped, conditional GET that skips unchanged pages.
- `hosts::Hosts`: the host policy: spacing between requests, a daily cap per site, and a shared backoff after a site blocks the pod.
- Extractors (`items::extract`): `events` (iCalendar and schema.org events), `json`, `embedded-json`, `jsonld`, `rss`, `ics`, `selectors` (CSS), with a small path language to map items to fields.
- `render::Browser`: a headless Chromium for pages that only fill in with JavaScript.
- `search`: the providers behind the `web_search` jack.
- `tasks` and `tools`: model tasks over web content (extract rows, research a row, pick from results), built for the agent module.
cards.heading: Its parts

cards.body: A feature builds a `Task::new(feature, tier, prompt)` with optional system text, a JSON schema for the answer, tools and a finishing tool, and calls `Agent::run(store, task)`. It gets an `Output {answer, finished, turns, …}` or an `AgentError` (`Unplugged`, `Budget`, `NoModel`, `Refused`, `CutOff`, `Failed`).
cards.heading: The interface

cards.body:
1. Refuse if the pod's `model` jack is unplugged.
2. Admit the call against the budgets: per feature, per pod (calls and tokens a day), and host-wide.
3. Pick the model: `Cheap` for computed fields, `Capable` for reading pages and research.
4. Send it, retrying rate limits, server errors and timeouts with backoff.
5. Run tools the model asks for (web fetch, search) until the finishing tool answers.

The server has one model key, `CONSTRUCT_INFER_API_KEY`, used by every model feature.
cards.heading: Inside a run

cards.body: `mcp_connect {name, url}` connects a server: at once if it needs nothing, with a sealed token, or through an OAuth sign-in the user opens in a browser. The pod lists its tools and calls only those the server marks read-only (others only when the user puts them on the server's allow list). A collection filler of kind `mcp` calls one on a schedule and maps its answer to rows. What a server answers is untrusted text.
cards.heading: How it works

cards.body:
- **In**: `dispatch(intent_json)` (what a tap does), `open_layout(id)`, `refresh`, `app_foregrounded`, sign-in redirects, staged attachments, device and push registration.
- **Out**: `subscribe(callback)` delivers immutable `StateSnapshot`s: the layout and every layout it reaches, entities and queries, connectivity, pending count, sign-in state, notifications.
- **Platform traits** a client implements: `SecureStore` (the keychain or keystore) and `UrlOpener` (the browser), plus a notification listener.
cards.heading: Its interface

cards.body:
- **The cache** (`cache.db`, SQLite): entities, data loads, construct objects, form values, notifications, so the last screen shows at once on launch and offline.
- **The outbox** (`action_outbox`): optimistic changes and their requests, written in one transaction, sent oldest first, rolled back on a refusal, retried on failure; one the pod keeps failing for 10 minutes is given up and rolled back, and `local://connection` says when changes are stuck and which were given up. A refetch re-applies changes still pending, so nothing flickers.
- **The event stream**: `/v1/construct/events`, reconnecting with backoff and catching up on reconnect.
- **Sign-in**: OAuth 2 with PKCE run by the engine itself, through a loopback port on desktop and an App Link on Android. Upstream tokens stay on the pod; the device keeps only its pod session.
cards.heading: Its parts

cards.body:
```
layout + entities + form,
route, theme
   │ layout: taffy flexbox,
   │ text by cosmic-text
   ▼
Scene: rounded quads, text
runs, a semantic tree
   │
   ├─▶ cpu: a distance function
   │   per pixel → PNG
   └─▶ gpu: wgpu + glyphon →
       window, surface, canvas
```
cards.heading: The pipeline

cards.body: `Session` (in `interact`) holds what is open: the root layout (home), one back stack of presented layouts and screens (pushed, sheets, panels, overlays, each animated), form values, scroll offsets and focus. It takes input (`tap`, `type_text`, `scroll_by`, gestures) and answers a scene. A new version of a layout replaces its tree where it is open, keeping open screens and scroll positions.
cards.heading: The session

cards.body:
- **`Loader`**: how a session gets layouts and data and sends intents. `PodEngine` implements it over the engine; the web client over `fetch`; the simulator over fixtures or a live pod.
- **`Platform`**: what it asks of the operating system: the keyboard, safe-area insets, opening links, the clipboard, picking photos, dark mode, notification permission. The desktop and Android apps implement it.
cards.heading: Its two interfaces

cards.body:
| Client | Where | Its platform layer |
|---|---|---|
| **Desktop** | `construct-viewer` (`--features viewer`); `scripts/macos_app.sh` makes the Mac app | A winit window, the loopback OAuth redirect, the login keychain |
| **Android** | a NativeActivity APK (`scripts/android_native.sh`, `android/`) | A small Java bridge that only forwards to Rust; the keystore; App Link sign-in; push through UnifiedPush |
| **Web** | `crates/construct-web`, served at `/web` with `CONSTRUCT_WEB=1` | WebAssembly in a canvas (WebGPU or WebGL2, else the CPU); a session cookie; no engine, its own loader |
| **Simulator** | `crates/construct-sim` | Headless, drawn on the CPU to PNGs from a script, against fixtures or a live pod |
| **Previews** | `pod_core::preview` | The pod draws a layout for the agent's `render_layout_preview` and taps it for `dispatch_virtual_interaction` |
cards.heading: The list

cards.body: One layout serves every window: the pod never sends a different layout per size. A layout uses `${local://device#size_class}` (`compact`, `medium`, `expanded`), `max_width_dp` and grid columns to use the room. A layout that uses none of them was written for a phone: the renderer draws it at most 480 points wide (centred on a screen of its own, against the pane before it when embedded or in a panel), so it stays phone-sized in a browser or beside a sidebar.
cards.heading: Screens of every size

cards.body:
| Job | Tools |
|---|---|
| Look around | `list_layouts`, `get_layout`, `find_elements`, `list_data_sources`, `sample_data`, `describe_vocabulary`, `guide` |
| Build screens | `create_layout`, `update_layout` (whole or JSON Patch), `validate_layout`, `define_component`, `copy_component`, `set_theme`, `restore_version` |
| Look at them | `render_layout_preview`, `dispatch_virtual_interaction`, `expand`, `walk_journey` (a whole journey replayed, writes as dry runs) |
| Change safely | `stage_edit_group`, `apply_edit_group`, `revert_edit_group`, `restore_checkpoint`, `usage_report`, `usage_paths` |
| Keep data | `define_collection`, `apply_change`, `edit_rows`, `add_row`, `describe_collection`, fillers (`collections_preview`, `collections_refresh`, `collections_status`), `undo_edit` |
| Abilities | `list_jacks`, `plug_jack`, `mcp_connect`, `mcp_servers` |
| Share | `publish`, `adopt`, `share_publicly`, `set_calendar_feed` |

Sources add their own (`agents_schedules`, `agents_link_tasks`). After the tool list changes, a Claude connector needs "Refresh tools list".
cards.heading: The tools by job

cards.body: Validation (against home's feeds and the sources' manifests, with a JSON pointer to each error), history (every version kept, `restore_version`), `warnings` (a hand-written piece a component already draws, fixed colours that won't follow dark mode), and live delivery to every device.
cards.heading: What every write gets

cards.body: The MCP instructions (under 2,000 characters) give the procedure: see what exists (`list_layouts`, `find_elements`); use a core layout whole when one fits; otherwise compose components; make a component of anything written twice; look at the result with a preview; say what was missing with `note_gap`, which the server's operator reads. `guide {topic}` holds the detail per topic (navigation, pages, components, theme, actions, jacks, sharing, and one per source).
cards.heading: The procedure

cards.body: A request about "my groceries screen" is about the element home reaches there, which may be the user's own copy of a core layout. `reached` and `copy_of` on every layout make that visible (decision `trace-from-home`).
cards.heading: Trace from home

cards.body:
| Crate | What it is |
|---|---|
| `protocol` | Wire types: `UiNode`, `ActionIntent`, `DataBundle`; `features/`, the named vocabulary |
| `construct-elements` | Elements, hashes, references, component expansion, materializing; shared by pod and engine |
| `pod-core` | The generic pod; `components/` holds the server components |
| `pod-host` | Many pods in one server: `host.db`, tokens, temporary pods, scheduler, shelf, public links |
| `server` | The binary and the `server pods` admin commands |
| `source-collections`, `source-pixelfed`, `source-events`, `source-agents`, `source-taste`, `source-monitor`, `source-dates`, `source-shell` | The sources; core layouts in `layouts/<id>/NNNN.json`, components in `components/` |
| `web-extract`, `agent` | The web module and the agent module |
| `client-core` | The engine |
| `construct-render` | The renderer, the desktop and Android apps, the pod's previews |
| `construct-web`, `construct-sim` | The web client and the headless simulator |
| `e2e`, `fake-pixelfed/` | The end-to-end suite and a fake Pixelfed to run it against |
| `design-lessons` | Reads this document into the course's JSON |
cards.heading: The crates

cards.body:
- **Unit and integration tests**: `cargo test --workspace`; each crate's integration tests are one binary, `tests/integration/main.rs`, with a module per file.
- **End to end** (`crates/e2e`): the pod and the engine in one process against the fake Pixelfed (or a real one), through a proxy that can be cut to test offline behaviour.
- **The simulator** (`construct-sim`): scripts like `click Like; assert-text Unlike; shot after` drive the real renderer and write PNGs; CI runs the scenarios and pull requests embed the screenshots.
- **Checks**: `cargo fmt`, `clippy -D warnings`, and scripts for decisions, test data (always made up) and old names.
cards.heading: The layers

cards.body:
1. **The core knows no source**: changes to a core layout are layout files plus source code.
2. **Layout and component files are append-only**: add the next `NNNN.json`; never edit a deployed one.
3. **Vocabulary is named features**: a new node type, intent or field needs a feature file and a client build.
4. **Migrations, not resets**: staging upgrades in place.
5. **Keep UI state across layout updates**: open screens and scroll positions survive a new version.
6. **Record decisions** in `docs/decisions/<topic>.md`, in the same pull request, and keep the guides current.
cards.heading: The rules

cards.body: [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/aidanwolter3/the-construct/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for setup and checks, [layouts.md](https://github.com/aidanwolter3/the-construct/blob/main/docs/layouts.md) to write layouts, [testing.md](https://github.com/aidanwolter3/the-construct/blob/main/docs/testing.md) and [simulator.md](https://github.com/aidanwolter3/the-construct/blob/main/docs/simulator.md) to check a change, [server.md](https://github.com/aidanwolter3/the-construct/blob/main/docs/server.md) to run it.
cards.heading: Where to go next

glossary.definition: an endpoint a source declares that intents may call, such as `/v1/collections/<c>/update`.

`crates/agent`, which every model call goes through.

`client-core`, the device's cache, outbox, sign-in and event stream.
one record a layout can bind, keyed by URI, such as `pixelfed://posts/101`.

an ability a pod can be plugged into: a switch, a config or an account.

what points at an element and keeps its history, such as `home` or `@me/card`.
the engine's queue of changes waiting to be sent to the pod.
the vocabulary the renderer draws: nodes, intents and device data.
one user's server: their layouts, data, sessions and sign-ins in one database.
the secret (`cpod_…`) that opens a pod; a device trades it for a pod session.
components, defined as data over plumbing and expanded before drawing.
a read-only web page copied from a layout and the rows it shows.
what a pod shares with other pods on the server, on the host's shelf.
an ordered list of entity URIs under a key, such as `collection:groceries`.
`construct-render`, which draws layouts on every client.
a part of a page layout opened by route, such as `collections://events/{id}`.
fix a reference to the element its name points at now, for a client's features.

a module of the pod that knows one kind of data, implementing `pod_core::Source` (once called an app adapter).
`crates/web-extract`, which every request to a website goes through.

lessons.summary: The Construct is a server-driven UI system: a server you own, the pod, decides what every screen of your apps looks like and holds your data, while native clients on your phone and computer only draw what the pod sends. Your agent (Claude) builds the screens by talking to the pod, so a new screen needs no app release.
lessons.title: The idea in one page
lessons.why: Every other part of the design follows from this split: the pod knows everything about your data, the clients know nothing about it, and the agent is how things get built.

lessons.summary: The design serves six goals; when two pull against each other, this order is roughly how they are weighed.
lessons.title: The goals

lessons.summary: Knowing what was left out makes the rest easier to read: there are no apps at runtime, no code in layouts, and no web view.
lessons.title: What it is not

lessons.summary: The system is a server half and a device half joined by HTTP, plus an agent that talks to the server over MCP. The server half is the pod and the abilities it is plugged into; the device half is one engine and one renderer shared by every client.
lessons.title: The map

lessons.summary: Opening the app shows how the pieces cooperate: the engine asks the pod for the root of its construct, fetches the elements it lacks, loads the data they bind, and hands both to the renderer, which draws them.
lessons.title: Following one screen
lessons.try_it: Run `cargo run -p construct-sim -- --workspace pixelfed_sample_no_login --out /tmp/sim --script "shot start"` and open `/tmp/sim`: that is steps 4 and 5 drawn from a fixture instead of a pod.

lessons.summary: Liking a photo shows the other direction: the renderer turns a tap into an intent, the engine applies it at once and queues it, the pod routes it to a source, and the source talks to the outside service.
lessons.title: Following one tap
lessons.try_it: In the simulator, `click Like; assert-text Unlike; shot liked` runs this whole path against a fake pod.

lessons.summary: The pieces meet at a handful of interfaces, and each one is narrow on purpose: knowing these seams is most of knowing the architecture.
lessons.title: The seams between pieces

lessons.summary: Three rules keep the pieces apart; most of the codebase's shape follows from them, and CONTRIBUTING.md lists them as rules to keep.
lessons.title: The rules everything follows

lessons.summary: A pod is everything one user has on the server: their layouts, their data, their sessions and sign-ins, and their notifications, all in one SQLite database. Its job is to serve layouts and data to that user's devices and agent, and to be the only place that talks to the outside world on their behalf.
lessons.title: The pod's job
lessons.why: Because the pod holds the sign-ins and does the fetching, devices never hold another service's token and never reach another host directly.

lessons.summary: The host (`crates/pod-host`) is what lets one server process serve many pods: it maps tokens to pods, makes temporary pods, wakes pods that have background work due, and holds what pods share. The `server` crate is the binary that puts the host and the sources together.
lessons.title: The host and the server binary
lessons.try_it: Make a temporary pod on staging (`curl -fsS -X POST https://the-construct-pod.fly.dev/v1/pods/temporary`) and read its construct with `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" https://the-construct-pod.fly.dev/v1/construct`. Delete it afterwards with `DELETE /v1/pods/temporary`.

lessons.summary: `pod-core` is the generic pod: about thirty modules, none of which knows any particular source. Grouping them by job makes it easy to find your way.
lessons.title: Inside pod-core

lessons.summary: Pods are opened lazily, so work that can't wait for a request is driven by the host's scheduler, and a source says when it needs the pod to stay open.
lessons.title: Background work

lessons.summary: The pod is the one place secrets and outside text meet, so the defaults are strict and most of them are enforced in one spot rather than left to each feature.
lessons.title: Security by construction

lessons.summary: A layout is a JSON tree of generic nodes (`core://Column`, `core://Text`, `core://List`, …) with intents attached to the parts you can tap. It binds to data by URI and field, and contains no code.
lessons.title: A layout is data
lessons.try_it: Ask your agent to `describe_vocabulary`, or read `crates/protocol/src/ast.rs`: every node type is one enum variant.

lessons.summary: Plumbing is what the renderer can draw: about thirty node types, a dozen intents, a small binding language and a set of device data. It lives in `crates/protocol`, and each piece is a named feature.
lessons.title: Plumbing: the vocabulary

lessons.summary: A component is a reusable piece of layout with parameters, defined as data and expanded into plumbing before it is drawn, so a whole design system can change with no client release.
lessons.title: Porcelain: components

lessons.summary: The construct is how a pod stores its layouts: every layout and component is an immutable **element** named by the hash of its JSON, **names** point at elements and keep history, and `home`'s hash stands for the whole tree. A device is up to date exactly when its root hash matches the pod's.
lessons.title: The construct
lessons.try_it: Ask your agent for `get_layout home`: its `history` is the list of elements the name `home` has pointed at, newest first.
lessons.why: Content addressing makes sync cheap and exact: a device fetches only the elements it hasn't seen, and an edit moves only the names it touched.

lessons.summary: Every piece of vocabulary is a named feature, and the pod serves each client the newest version of each name that it can fully draw. That is how a layout can use something new without breaking a phone that hasn't updated.
lessons.title: Features: keeping old clients working

lessons.summary: Every pod's interface is what `home` reaches. Home starts as a blank page; the agent adds layouts that reference or copy core layouts, and home embeds or opens them.
lessons.title: Home, core layouts and the agent's layouts

lessons.summary: A pod can share what it built three ways: a **publication** another pod adopts and binds to its own data, a **public link** anyone can open in a browser, and a **calendar feed** for calendar apps. Each answers a review first.
lessons.title: Sharing between people

lessons.summary: A source implements one trait, `pod_core::Source` (`crates/pod-core/src/adapter.rs`), and through it declares everything the pod and layouts may use: its feeds, screen data and actions, its routes and tables, its notification channels, its jacks, and the core layouts and components it ships.
lessons.title: What a source is
lessons.try_it: Ask your agent for `list_data_sources`: every source's manifest, as layouts see it.
lessons.why: The trait is the only way the pod meets a source, so a new kind of data is a new crate that implements it, with no change to the core.

lessons.summary: All data travels in one shape: **entities** keyed by URI, and **queries**, ordered lists of URIs. A source fills them; the engine caches them; a layout's lists and bindings read them.
lessons.title: Entities, feeds and the data bundle

lessons.summary: Collections (`crates/source-collections`) is the source for data the user keeps themselves: the agent declares a collection's typed fields, and the pod stores, validates, computes and serves the rows. It is the source most layouts are built on.
lessons.title: Collections
lessons.try_it: Ask your agent to "keep a log of my car's oil changes and show it on home": it will declare a collection, write a layout for it and add the layout to home.

lessons.summary: The Pixelfed source (`crates/source-pixelfed`) is a full client of a Pixelfed photo-sharing server, and the reference for a source that talks to an outside service: its own sign-in, routes, tables, polls and core layout.
lessons.title: Pixelfed

lessons.summary: The other sources show the range of what a source can be: one built entirely on Collections, one that mirrors an outside runner, one that keeps a page of an outside service's feed, and three that are mostly layouts.
lessons.title: Events, Agents, Taste and the small sources

lessons.summary: Notifications are a shared service of the pod: any source hands it a ready-made notification on a channel it declared, and the pod stores it, delivers it to every device, and works out which layout should open it.
lessons.title: Notifications across sources

lessons.summary: A jack is an ability a pod can be plugged into or unplugged from, like a socket on a synthesizer: a switch (on or off), a config (a provider and a sealed key), or an account (a sign-in a source declares). Features check the jack before they use the ability (decision `jacks`).
lessons.title: What a jack is
lessons.track_title: Jacks, the web module and the agent module
lessons.try_it: Ask your agent for `list_jacks` to see what your pod is plugged into.
lessons.why: One place decides whether a pod may spend model calls or touch the web, so a host can lock abilities off for a temporary pod and a user can turn them off in Settings.

lessons.summary: Every request to a website goes through `crates/web-extract`: fetching, reading structured data out of pages, the per-host policy, search providers, and the prompts used when a model reads web text (decision `web-and-agent-modules`).
lessons.title: The web module
lessons.track_title: Jacks, the web module and the agent module

lessons.summary: Every model call goes through `crates/agent` (`construct-agent`): it checks the `model` jack, counts the call against daily budgets, picks the model for the task's tier, retries, and runs the tool loop.
lessons.title: The agent module
lessons.track_title: Jacks, the web module and the agent module

lessons.summary: Besides being an MCP server for the agent, a pod can be a client of other MCP servers (the `mcp` jack, decision `mcp-jack`), so a collection can be filled from another service's tools.
lessons.title: The pod as an MCP client
lessons.track_title: Jacks, the web module and the agent module

lessons.summary: The engine (`crates/client-core`, `ConstructEngine`) is the device's brain: it holds a local cache of everything loaded, an outbox of changes waiting to be sent, the pod session and upstream sign-ins, and the live event stream. The renderer only ever sees its snapshots.
lessons.title: The engine
lessons.why: Offline use, instant taps and live updates are all the engine's work; a client gets them by using it, not by writing them again.

lessons.summary: The renderer (`crates/construct-render`) turns a plumbing layout and its data into pixels, in Rust, on the GPU or the CPU. It is the only renderer: every client and the pod's previews use it.
lessons.title: The renderer
lessons.try_it: `scripts/sim_scenarios.sh /tmp/sim` draws the scenarios CI screenshots, through this same pipeline.

lessons.summary: Each client is the renderer plus a thin layer for its platform; none has screens of its own beyond a bundled sign-in page, because Settings and the inbox are layouts too.
lessons.title: The clients

lessons.summary: Each pod serves MCP at `POST /v1/mcp`. A Claude app connects to it as a custom connector (OAuth, then the user types their pod code), Claude Code with a credential from `server pods mcp`. The credential reaches only that pod's MCP endpoint.
lessons.title: The pod's MCP server
lessons.try_it: Ask your agent to `render_layout_preview` your home: it sees the screen as your phone draws it.

lessons.summary: The pod teaches the agent as it goes: short instructions with a build procedure, a guide per topic, a catalog of what exists, and warnings on every write. The aim is that the agent reuses what exists and changes what the user sees.
lessons.title: How an agent is taught

lessons.summary: The repository is one Rust workspace: the wire types, the pod and its host, the sources, the two shared modules, the engine, the renderer and its clients, and the test tools.
lessons.title: The repository

lessons.summary: Every crate has unit tests and one integration test binary; the end-to-end suite runs the real pod and engine together; the simulator checks screens as PNGs. There are no emulator or device tests, so a change that needs a device says so.
lessons.title: Testing

lessons.summary: A few rules protect the design, and most mistakes they prevent are ones a first change would make: editing a deployed layout file, teaching the core about a source, or resetting a database.
lessons.title: Changing things safely

tracks.summary: The Construct is a way to have native apps that are entirely your own: their screens and data live on your own server, and your agent builds them by asking.
tracks.title: Why it exists

tracks.summary: A handful of big pieces make up the system: the pod on its host, the sources and jacks inside it, the construct of layouts, the engine and renderer on each device, and the agent that builds.
tracks.title: The big pieces

tracks.summary: The pod is one user's server; the host runs many pods in one process. This part opens both.
tracks.title: The pod and its host

tracks.summary: A layout is a screen written as data. This part covers the vocabulary layouts are written in, the components built on it, and the construct: how a pod stores layouts so devices fetch only what changed.
tracks.title: Layouts and the construct

tracks.summary: A source is a module of the pod that knows one kind of data. This part explains the `Source` interface, the data it serves, and each source in the repository.
tracks.title: Data sources

tracks.summary: Some abilities are shared by many features: calling a model, fetching a web page, searching, calling an MCP server, using an account. Jacks say which of them a pod is plugged into; two modules make every web request and model call go one way.
tracks.title: Jacks, the web module and the agent module

tracks.summary: On each device, one engine and one renderer do everything; each client is a thin shell of platform code around them.
tracks.title: The device side

tracks.summary: The agent is how anything gets built: Claude connects to the pod's MCP server and reads, writes and looks at layouts and collections. This part covers that server and how an agent is taught to use it well.
tracks.title: Building with an agent

tracks.summary: This part is for changing the code: where things are, how they are tested, and the rules that keep the design intact.
tracks.title: Working on the codebase
